title: Stream processing and backpressure
scopeHtml: Scope: windows, watermarks, lag, DLQ and retries.

notes.title: What stream processing is
notes.html:
Stream processing computes results continuously as events arrive, instead of waiting to run a batch job on yesterday's data. Examples: fraud score in 200 ms, a live dashboard of orders per minute, ETA updates.

Typical stack: Kafka as the source, a processor (Kafka Streams, Apache Flink, Spark Structured Streaming), state held locally (RocksDB) and checkpointed, results written to Kafka, a DB or a cache.

Worked example. Count orders per city per minute from 5,000 events/s. State is a map of (city, minute) to count: say 500 cities x a few open windows, a few thousand entries, tiny. The hard part is not memory but late and out-of-order events.

Industry examples. Uber (Flink for surge and marketplace metrics), Netflix (Flink pipelines), LinkedIn (Samza and Kafka Streams), Alibaba (Flink for Singles' Day dashboards).

Everyday analogy. A toll-booth counter that updates the total after every car, instead of counting tickets at midnight.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing streaming where an hourly batch is enough; streaming costs more to operate.
  • Ignoring state: where it lives, how big, how it recovers.

notes.title: Windows
notes.html:
A window groups an unbounded stream into finite chunks you can aggregate.

  • Tumbling: fixed, non-overlapping (00:00 to 00:01, 00:01 to 00:02).
  • Sliding (hopping): fixed size, moves by a smaller step (5-minute window every 1 minute); each event lands in several windows.
  • Session: closes after a gap of inactivity (for example 30 minutes without a click); length varies per user.
Tumbling 1 min:  [0-1)[1-2)[2-3)
Sliding 3m/1m:   [0-3)
                   [1-4)
                     [2-5)
Session gap 5m:  click click   (gap)   click click click
                 |--session 1--|        |---session 2---|

Worked example. Sliding 5-minute window every 1 minute over 10,000 events/s: each event is in 5 windows, so aggregation work multiplies by 5. Flink optimises this with panes or incremental aggregation.

Industry examples. Sessionisation of user activity (Spotify, e-commerce analytics), per-minute metrics (Datadog-style), anomaly detection with sliding windows.

Everyday analogy. Counting traffic per hour (tumbling), "last 60 minutes, updated each minute" (sliding), or one visit to a shop from entering to leaving (session).

Common interview traps.

  • Using processing time when business correctness needs event time.
  • Large sliding windows with tiny steps, which multiplies compute and state.

notes.title: Event time, watermarks and late data
notes.html:
Event time is when the thing happened (a timestamp from the phone). Processing time is when the system saw it. Mobile events arrive late: a user goes through a tunnel and the click arrives 3 minutes after it happened.

A watermark is the processor's claim "I believe no events older than time T will arrive any more". When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window fires. Typical rule: watermark = max event time seen - allowed lateness bound (for example 10 s).

Trade-off: a long delay gives correct results but high latency; a short delay gives fast results but drops or corrects late events. Options for later arrivals: drop, send to a side output, or allow allowedLateness and emit an updated result.

# Flink-style idea (PyFlink-like pseudocode)
stream.assign_timestamps_and_watermarks(
    WatermarkStrategy.for_bounded_out_of_orderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10)))

Worked example. Window 12:00 to 12:01, watermark lag 10 s. The window fires when an event with time 12:01:10 is seen. A click stamped 12:00:30 arriving at 12:01:20 is late: handled by allowed lateness (update) or side output.

Gravity. The watermark bound is a tunable choice you can revisit, but changing it changes output semantics (and results already emitted). Idle partitions can stall watermarks; use idleness timeouts.

Industry examples. Google Dataflow/Beam model (the paper "The Dataflow Model") introduced this language; Flink implements it.

Everyday analogy. Closing exam submissions: you wait a few minutes after the deadline for students stuck in the queue, then stop.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing watermark with the current time.
  • One idle partition holding back the global watermark.
  • Dropping late data silently with no metric.

notes.title: Consumer lag and backpressure
notes.html:
Consumer lag = how many messages (or seconds) the consumer is behind the producer. It is the most important health number for a streaming system. Rising lag means consumers are slower than producers.

Backpressure is the system slowing producers or upstream stages because a downstream stage cannot keep up. In Kafka the log itself is the buffer, so producers are never blocked by slow consumers: lag just grows (until retention deletes data you have not read!). In Flink, bounded network buffers propagate backpressure upstream to the source, which then reads slower.

Handling rising lag:

  1. Check if it is a sudden spike (burst) or a trend.
  2. Scale consumers up to the partition count.
  3. Fix the slow part (DB calls per message; batch them; async I/O).
  4. Increase partitions if consumers already equal partitions.
  5. Shed or sample low-value work.

Worked example. Produce 10,000 msg/s, consume 6,000 msg/s: lag grows 4,000/s = 14.4M per hour. With 7-day retention you have time, but with 1-hour retention you would lose data after about 1 hour. Alert on lag in time (lag / consume rate) and on the lag growth rate, not just absolute count.

Industry examples. Tools: Burrow (LinkedIn), Kafka Lag Exporter, Confluent Control Center, CloudWatch for MSK. Uber and others alert on end-to-end latency using event timestamps.

Everyday analogy. A sink with the tap on faster than the drain: the water level (lag) rises, and when it overflows (retention) you lose water.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming Kafka pushes back on producers; it does not, it buffers.
  • Scaling consumers beyond partition count.
  • Alerting only on absolute lag, which is meaningless at different rates.

notes.title: Retries, dead-letter queues and poison messages
notes.html:
Some messages fail: transient (DB down) or permanent (bad data, a "poison pill"). Retrying a permanent failure blocks the partition forever, since Kafka consumers process in order.

Pattern:

  1. Retry transient errors a few times with exponential backoff (for example 1 s, 5 s, 30 s) and jitter.
  2. After N attempts, publish the message plus error info (original topic, partition, offset, exception) to a dead-letter topic/queue and commit and move on.
  3. Alert on DLQ depth; fix the bug; replay from the DLQ.

For ordered streams, non-blocking retries use separate retry topics (orders.retry.1m, orders.retry.10m) so the main partition keeps flowing, at the cost of reordering.

# Spring Kafka style idea
retry: { attempts: 4, backoff: { initial: 1s, multiplier: 5, max: 60s } }
dead-letter-topic: orders.dlq

Worked example. One malformed JSON message at offset 8,421 throws on every attempt. With infinite retry, 3 million later messages are stuck behind it and lag explodes. After 3 attempts it goes to orders.dlq and consumption continues; on-call fixes the parser and replays 1 message.

Industry examples. Uber's blog on reliable reprocessing with retry topics and DLQs; SQS has native DLQs via maxReceiveCount.

Everyday analogy. A parcel with a wrong address goes into a "problem" bin instead of blocking the conveyor belt.

Common interview traps.

  • Infinite retry loops and head-of-line blocking.
  • A DLQ nobody monitors; it becomes a data graveyard.
  • Retrying without idempotency, so a side effect happens twice.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Stream processing = continuous computation with local, checkpointed state (Flink, Kafka Streams).
  • Windows: tumbling, sliding, session; sliding multiplies work.
  • Use event time with watermarks; the bound trades latency vs completeness; handle late data explicitly.
  • Lag (best in seconds) is the health metric; Kafka buffers instead of blocking producers; scale to partition count, then fix the handler.
  • Retry with backoff, then DLQ; use retry topics to avoid blocking; always monitor the DLQ.

questions.promptHtml: What is stream processing, how does it differ from a nightly batch job, and when would you NOT use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks judgment: streaming is costly to run, so the right answer includes when to avoid it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stream processing computes results continuously as events arrive, so a fraud score can be ready in 200 ms or a dashboard can update every few seconds. Batch waits and processes a bounded chunk, like yesterday's data. I use streaming when the value of the result decays fast, and batch when an hourly or daily result is enough, because streaming adds state, checkpoints and 24/7 operations.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A typical stack: Kafka as the source, a processor (Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Structured Streaming), local state (often RocksDB) checkpointed for recovery, output to Kafka, a DB or a cache. State is the hard part: where it lives, how big, how it recovers. For 5,000 events/s counting per city per minute, state is a few thousand entries, tiny; the hard problems are late and out-of-order events, not memory.

Kafka topic -> Stream processor (state store, checkpoints) -> Output topic / DB

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using streaming where an hourly batch is enough.
  • Ignoring state size and recovery time.
  • Treating it as "a faster batch" and ignoring time semantics.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is lambda vs kappa architecture? -> Lambda runs batch and stream in parallel; kappa uses one streaming path with replay for reprocessing.
  2. How does a stream job recover from a crash? -> Restore state from the last checkpoint/changelog and re-read from the checkpointed offset.
  3. How do you reprocess history? -> Replay from the log with a new job version, compare outputs, then switch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "real-time vs batch". Senior: cost-of-operating, state and recovery, time semantics and when batch wins.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team built a Flink pipeline for a report nobody opened more than once a day; a cron SQL job would have cost a tenth.

questions.promptHtml: Explain tumbling, sliding and session windows. Which would you use for "orders per minute", "rolling 5-minute average updated every minute" and "user visit length"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic vocabulary of streaming; the senior signal is cost awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, so "orders per minute". Sliding windows have a fixed size but move by a smaller step, so each event lands in several windows: the rolling 5-minute average every minute. Session windows close after a gap of inactivity, so their length varies per user: "visit length".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tumbling 1 min:  [0-1)[1-2)[2-3)
Sliding 3m/1m:   [0-3)
                   [1-4)
                     [2-5)
Session gap 5m:  click click   (gap)   click click click
                 |--session 1--|        |---session 2---|

Sliding with size/step = k puts each event in k windows, multiplying compute and state by k. Engines mitigate with incremental aggregation or panes. Session windows merge when a late event bridges two sessions, so they are the most complex to maintain.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using processing-time windows when the business needs event time.
  • Large sliding windows with tiny steps.
  • Forgetting session windows are per key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cost of sliding 5 min / 1 s step? -> Each event in 300 windows; consider an incremental structure or a coarser step.
  2. How do session windows handle late data? -> They can merge adjacent sessions.
  3. Can you get a rolling average without sliding windows? -> Yes: tumbling sub-aggregates (sum, count) per minute, combined on read.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the three. Senior: ties each to a requirement, quantifies the multiplier and offers the sub-aggregate trick.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 1-hour/1-second sliding window multiplied state 3,600x and OOMed the job; moving to per-minute sub-aggregates fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A PM says: "Show me how many users are active right now." The product has 2M daily users and 8,000 events/s at peak. Events carry a user id and an event timestamp.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts coding a "count distinct users in the last hour" without defining "active" or "right now".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What counts as active (any event? login?) and for how long (1, 5, 30 min)? How fresh must the number be (1 s or 1 min)? Exact or approximate? Per region?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is requirements clarification.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Likely "distinct users with an event in the last 5 minutes, refreshed every 10-30 s".
  4. How I'd verify: Agree on the definition with the PM, then compare against a one-off SQL on raw events.
  5. Root cause (design): A sliding window of 5 minutes with a 10 s step over distinct user ids, keyed globally; with 8k events/s, exact distinct state is up to about 8k x 300 = 2.4M entries, fine, or use HyperLogLog (error about 1-2%) to shrink it.
  6. Fix (build): Kafka source, event-time sliding window 5m/10s, HLL aggregate, output to Redis for the dashboard; watermark of 10 s.
  7. Prevention: Document the metric definition; backfill test with known counts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not exact distinct on the entire stream with unbounded state; not a session window (that answers a different question).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM now wants 30-day active users? -> Not a streaming window; use a daily batch or bitmap/HLL store.
  • Events arrive up to 2 minutes late? -> Raise the watermark bound or use allowed lateness.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: two teams reported different "active users" for a year because the window definition was never written down.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts coding.
  • Hire: clarifies and picks a sliding window.
  • Strong hire: quantifies state, proposes HLL, covers lateness and metric definition.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between event time and processing time, and what is a watermark? How do you handle late events?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common streaming-correctness question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Event time is when the thing happened (the phone's timestamp); processing time is when my system saw it. A watermark is the processor's claim that no events older than T will arrive, normally max event time seen - allowed bound. When it passes the end of a window, the window fires. The bound trades latency against completeness, and late events are dropped, sent to a side output or applied as an update with allowed lateness.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mobile clients go offline and flush later, so arrival order differs from event order. Window correctness for business numbers requires event time. With a 10 s bound, window 12:00-12:01 fires when an event stamped 12:01:10 is seen. A click stamped 12:00:30 that arrives at 12:01:20 is late. Each option has a cost: dropping loses data, side output needs a reconciliation job, allowed lateness emits corrections (downstream must handle updates, so the sink should be an upsert).

# PyFlink-like idea
stream.assign_timestamps_and_watermarks(
    WatermarkStrategy.for_bounded_out_of_orderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10)))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing the watermark with the wall clock.
  • Dropping late data silently with no metric.
  • Forgetting idle partitions stall the watermark.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you pick the bound? -> Measure the lateness distribution (p99) and balance against latency SLO.
  2. What does the sink need for allowed lateness? -> Idempotent upserts keyed by window.
  3. What if one partition is idle? -> The minimum watermark across inputs stalls; use idleness timeouts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: measures lateness, plans corrections, and knows the idle-partition trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard understated mobile revenue until the team added a side output and a nightly correction.

questions.contextHtml:
Pager: "orders-consumer lag 2.1M". Producers write 10,000 msg/s and consumers handle 6,000 msg/s since a deploy 30 minutes ago. Topic retention is 1 hour. The DB team says the DB is healthy.

consumer-group orders-cg
PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
0          81,203,110      81,950,004      746,894
1          80,000,515      80,200,100      199,585
...

Lag is uneven across partitions.
questions.promptHtml: How much time do you have, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds more consumers blindly or only watches absolute lag.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the deploy? Is it constant or a spike? Consumers vs partitions count? Is the uneven lag a hot key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compute the deadline: lag grows 4,000/s, retention 1 h. Raise retention temporarily (kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config retention.ms=...) to protect data; roll back the deploy if it slowed handling.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) new code is slower (per-message DB call); (b) hot key on partition 0; (c) fewer consumers (crash loop); (d) DB is the red herring since it reports healthy.
  4. How I'd verify: Profile the handler; per-partition consumer rates; deploy diff; consumer count and rebalances.
  5. Root cause: Consume rate below produce rate: lag grows 4,000/s = 14.4M per hour, so the oldest unprocessed data hits the 1-hour retention edge and starts being deleted.
  6. Fix: Short term: rollback, scale consumers up to the partition count. Long term: batch DB writes, async I/O, repartition if consumers equal partitions, handle hot keys.
  7. Prevention: Alert on lag in seconds (lag / consume rate) and lag growth rate, and on lag as a fraction of retention.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not scaling past partition count (idle consumers), not skipping to latest to "clear lag" (data loss).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lag is 0 but dashboards are stale? -> Check the processor's output, or end-to-end latency using event timestamps.
  • How to catch up faster? -> Temporary extra consumers and relaxed non-critical work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: lag recovered only after retention was extended; without it, 40 minutes of orders would have been deleted unread.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds consumers only.
  • Hire: computes growth and retention deadline.
  • Strong hire: protects data first, alerts in time units, and analyses uneven partitions.

questions.contextHtml:
At 03:12 the orders consumer stops making progress: lag grows 3,000/s on partition 5 only, other partitions are fine. Logs:

ERROR OrderHandler - Failed offset=8421 partition=5: JsonParseException: Unexpected character ('<')
INFO  Retrying offset=8421 (attempt 1412)

The handler has while(true) retry on any exception.
questions.promptHtml: Fix it now and design it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restarts the consumer or skips the offset manually with no record.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the failure transient or permanent? Which producer sent HTML into a JSON topic? Does ordering on this partition matter?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the bad record to a dead-letter topic (with topic, partition, offset, exception) and commit past it, e.g. via a quick patch or kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --shift-by 1 after copying the payload out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Poison pill from an upstream bug; schema change; truncated message. The < suggests an HTML error page published as an event.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the raw bytes of offset 8421 (kafka-console-consumer.sh --partition 5 --offset 8421 --max-messages 1).
  5. Root cause: An unbounded retry on a permanent error causes head-of-line blocking since Kafka consumers process a partition in order.
  6. Fix: Classify errors: transient get bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter (1 s, 5 s, 30 s); permanent go straight to orders.dlq and commit. Use retry topics (orders.retry.1m) if the main flow must keep going, accepting reordering.
  7. Prevention: Alert on DLQ depth and age, schema validation at the producer, replay tooling, contract tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not silently dropping the record, and not leaving a DLQ unmonitored (a graveyard).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if order matters per key? -> Park the key in a retry path and hold its later events, or accept bounded blocking.
  • Retried side effects? -> Need idempotency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: one bad record held 3M messages for 40 minutes until someone manually moved offsets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart or infinite retry.
  • Hire: DLQ with bounded retries.
  • Strong hire: error classification, replay path, ordering trade-offs and DLQ monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A Flink job computes a per-user "events in the last 10 minutes" using a sliding window 10 min / 1 s step at 5,000 events/s. It works at present, but traffic will grow 10x for a campaign. Heap use is already 70% and checkpoint time is 40 s.
questions.promptHtml: Will it survive 10x? What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more memory", without noticing the 600x window multiplier.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How fresh must the number be (1 s or 10 s)? Exact or approximate? Per user or global? What is the checkpoint interval SLO?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Increase the step to 10 s to cut the multiplier 10x before the campaign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each event lands in 600 windows; at 50,000 events/s that is 30M window updates/s; state and checkpoints scale with it.
  4. How I'd verify: Flink state size metrics, checkpoint duration, backpressure indicators.
  5. Root cause: Window cost is size/step times event rate; 10 min / 1 s = 600x.
  6. Fix: Pre-aggregate into 10-second tumbling buckets per user, keep the last 60 buckets and sum on emit (60x less), or use a managed incremental sliding aggregate; use RocksDB incremental checkpoints.
  7. Prevention: Load test at 2x the expected peak; track state size growth.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "more memory" alone; a 10 s resolution is the accuracy price.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exactness needed per second? -> Keep fine buckets only for the last minute.
  • Skewed users? -> Salt hot keys and combine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a fine-grained window was fine at launch and fell over at the first sale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds memory.
  • Hire: spots the multiplier and enlarges the step.
  • Strong hire: bucketed pre-aggregation with quantified savings and checkpoint awareness.

questions.promptHtml: What is backpressure? Compare how it works with a Kafka consumer versus inside a Flink job, and what you do when lag keeps rising.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that Kafka buffers instead of pushing back, and what that means for retention and operations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Backpressure is a slow downstream stage forcing upstream to slow down. Kafka never pushes back on producers: the log is the buffer, so lag simply grows until retention deletes unread data. Inside Flink, bounded network buffers propagate backpressure upstream to the source, which then reads Kafka more slowly. When lag rises, I check whether it is a burst or a trend, scale consumers to the partition count, fix the slow handler (batch, async I/O), then add partitions or shed low-value work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Produce 10k/s vs consume 6k/s gives lag growth of 4,000/s = 14.4M per hour. With 7-day retention this is a capacity issue; with 1-hour retention it is data loss within an hour. Lag should be alerted in time (lag / consume rate) plus growth rate, since absolute numbers mean little at different throughputs. Scaling consumers beyond partition count yields idle consumers.

Producer 10k/s -> (Kafka log) -> Consumer 6k/s   => lag +4k/s
Flink: Sink slow -> buffers fill -> operators block -> source reads slower

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Kafka slows producers.
  • Alerting only on absolute lag.
  • More consumers than partitions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to find the slow Flink operator? -> Backpressure/busy-time metrics in the UI; the first non-backpressured downstream operator is the bottleneck.
  2. When is shedding load acceptable? -> Low-value analytics, with explicit sampling and metrics.
  3. How does lag interact with exactly-once checkpoints? -> Longer checkpoints under backpressure can delay commits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "scale consumers". Senior: retention deadline, time-based alerts, bottleneck isolation and load shedding.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A lag alert at 1M was ignored as "normal" at 50k/s; at 5k/s the same lag was a 3-minute delay in fraud scoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A Flink job windows per minute over a topic with 12 partitions and 4,000 events/s. After a regional rollout at 02:00, output windows freeze at 01:58 for 25 minutes although events keep flowing. No errors. Partition stats:

partition 0..10: ~360 events/s each
partition 11   : 0 events/s since 01:58 (producer for that shard stopped)
checkpoint OK, backpressure OK, lag normal
questions.promptHtml: Why are no windows firing, and how do you fix and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restarts the job or blames Kafka.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What watermark strategy is used? Is there per-partition watermarking? Did a producer shard stop (red herring: Kafka is fine)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Configure an idleness timeout or temporarily restart with withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1)).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Idle partition holding the global watermark (min across inputs); a stuck timestamp extractor; clock issue.
  4. How I'd verify: Check the watermark metric per source subtask; confirm partition 11's watermark is stuck at 01:58.
  5. Root cause: The operator's watermark is the minimum across its inputs; an idle partition never advances, so windows never close.
  6. Fix: WatermarkStrategy...withIdleness(...); heartbeats/keep-alive events from producers.
  7. Prevention: Alert on watermark lag (wall-clock minus watermark) and on silent partitions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: With idleness a revived partition's late events are treated as late data; I accept that and route them to a side output. I would not drop the watermark bound to zero.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does low traffic at night cause it? -> Same mechanism with sparse keys.
  • Processing-time windows instead? -> Fire regardless, but results are wrong when events are delayed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a staging environment with one active partition hid this until production traffic skewed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts.
  • Hire: identifies idle partition and idleness timeout.
  • Strong hire: adds watermark-lag alerting, late-data handling and producer heartbeats.

questions.contextHtml: A mobile app emits events; 98% arrive within 5 s, 99.9% within 3 minutes, a tail up to 6 hours (offline users). Finance needs hourly revenue by region, and the live dashboard needs 1-minute freshness. The team sets a 6-hour watermark delay "to be correct".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either keep the 6-hour delay (dashboard dead) or use 5 seconds and drop the tail without telling anyone.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the live view allowed to be approximate and later corrected? Is the finance number final at some deadline? Can the sink accept updates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two consumers with different needs cannot share one latency/completeness point.
  4. How I'd verify: Compute the lateness histogram from real data (p50, p99, p99.9).
  5. Root cause: A single watermark conflates "fast approximate" and "slow exact".
  6. Fix: Live path: watermark 10 s, allowedLateness 5 min emitting updated results; late tail beyond that goes to a side output into the lake; finance path: a batch/stream job that recomputes the hourly revenue after 6-12 hours (or upserts corrections). Sink is an upsert keyed by (region, window).
  7. Prevention: Metrics for late-event counts and correction volume; document the semantics ("preliminary" vs "final").
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not silently dropping; not delaying the dashboard 6 hours.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retractions required downstream? -> Emit versioned updates or use a changelog.
  • Cost of corrections? -> Small at 0.1% tail volume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: revenue was 0.4% under-reported for months because late data was dropped with no counter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one watermark for all.
  • Hire: separates live and final paths.
  • Strong hire: data-driven bound, upserts, side output and labelled semantics.

questions.contextHtml:
A notification consumer calls a flaky SMS vendor (3% of calls fail transiently, vendor outages of 10 minutes happen). Volume: 2,000 msg/s. Currently: 5 immediate retries then crash. During the last outage all consumers crash-looped and caused a retry storm on the vendor when it recovered:

12:04 vendor 503  ->  consumers retry 5x with no delay -> 10,000 calls/s
12:05 consumers crash, restart, reprocess same batch
12:15 vendor recovers, sees 40,000 calls/s, rate limits (429)

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase retry count" or "sleep 1 second".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does per-user order of SMS matter? Max acceptable delay? Is the vendor call idempotent (idempotency key supported)? Vendor rate limit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a circuit breaker and a rate limiter; pause consumption (pause()) while open.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Synchronous immediate retries amplify load (retry storm); crash-loop re-delivers the same batch; no jitter synchronises consumers.
  4. How I'd verify: Vendor call rate graph; consumer restart counts; retry histogram.
  5. Root cause: Retries without backoff/jitter, no breaker, and failure handling by crashing.
  6. Fix: Exponential backoff with jitter (1 s, 5 s, 30 s); non-blocking retry topics (sms.retry.1m, sms.retry.10m) so the main partition keeps flowing; DLQ after the last tier; a circuit breaker and token-bucket limit matched to the vendor quota; idempotency key per message to avoid double SMS.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test vendor outages; alert on retry-topic depth and DLQ age.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Retry topics reorder messages; if per-user order matters I accept bounded blocking for that key or a state check ("is this older than the last sent?"). I would not retry infinitely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• OTP SMS with a 60 s validity? -> Skip long retry tiers; fail fast and let the user resend.
  • Vendor does not support idempotency keys? -> Record a send log before the call and accept rare duplicates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a recovered vendor was knocked over again by the backlog replay of its own customers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more retries.
  • Hire: backoff, retry topics, DLQ.
  • Strong hire: breaker and rate limiting, ordering and idempotency trade-offs, business-aware tiers.

questions.contextHtml: A topic has 24 partitions, 24 consumers (each 4 vCPU, 8 GB), handling 48,000 msg/s; each message does one DB lookup (4 ms) and one HTTP call (6 ms). Peak lag stays at 0 but the cloud bill is high and CPU is 15%. Next quarter volume doubles, and the topic cannot exceed 24 partitions without a migration.
questions.promptHtml: How do you serve 96,000 msg/s without 48 consumers or repartitioning?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Double the pods and the partitions."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must per-key ordering be preserved? Can the DB and HTTP calls be batched or cached? What are the latency SLOs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; planning.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each consumer does 48,000/24 = 2,000 msg/s at 10 ms of waiting per message, so it already needs about 20 concurrent calls in flight; at 96k it needs about 40. CPU at 15% says the limiter is waiting on I/O, not computing, so the lever is concurrency and batching per consumer, not more pods.
  4. How I'd verify: Thread dump, handler timing, DB/HTTP latency percentiles, connection pool saturation.
  5. Root cause: Low CPU with high wait means concurrency per consumer is under-used.
  6. Fix: Process records of one poll concurrently with a worker pool keyed by message key (preserves per-key order), use async I/O, batch the DB lookups (WHERE id IN (...)), cache hot lookups, commit the lowest contiguous completed offset. With 4 vCPU and mostly waiting, the same 24 pods can carry the 2x load.
  7. Prevention: Load test with realistic latencies; track per-consumer concurrency and pool waits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: In-process concurrency adds offset-tracking complexity and the risk of duplicates on crash (idempotent handlers needed); repartitioning is the last resort because of key remapping.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Downstream DB now the bottleneck? -> Batch, cache, read replicas, backpressure with pause().
  • Strict global ordering? -> Then partitions are the ceiling; redesign the ordering requirement.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team halved infrastructure cost by batching lookups, without adding any partitions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale pods/partitions.
  • Hire: identifies I/O wait and adds concurrency/batching.
  • Strong hire: preserves key ordering, handles offset tracking, quantifies gains and names fallback.
